title: The role of trade unions in the economy

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Explain the roles trade unions play in the economy, and keep a union's work apart from bodies that promote trade.

blocks.heading: What unions do
blocks.text: A union's first role is collective bargaining: it negotiates with the employer over the pay and working conditions of all its members at once. Around that core sit the other roles: protecting members' rights, representing them in disputes such as an unfair dismissal or a disagreement over shift patterns, and pressing for safer workplaces and training that raises members' skills. A settlement at a large workplace also tends to shape pay in the same trade elsewhere, because employers nearby compete for the same workers and are likely to match the rate. That is why unions matter to the economy and not merely to one firm: through many local bargains they influence wages across the labour market.

blocks.heading: One bargain at a cannery
blocks.text: At Kuiseb Fish Processors, a cannery in Walvis Bay, 240 of the 300 workers belong to the Marine Workers' Union. In 2026 the union negotiated an hourly rise from N$12.50 to N$14.00, and the cannery paid the higher rate to all 300. One member alone is a single worker among three hundred; the union, speaking for 240 of them, is a party the cannery has to take seriously, because replacing a workforce of that size would halt the plant. It extended the rise to non-members too, since two pay rates in one cannery breed resentment. In Germany, the union at a Hamburg bus company bargains the same way: one agreement covers the drivers' pay and shift rosters.

blocks.heading: Bargaining over hours, and protecting jobs
blocks.text: Collective bargaining covers more than pay. Unions negotiate working hours: the length of the working week and of each shift, rest breaks, how much overtime can be demanded, and the rate it is paid at. Security guards at Namib Guarding in Windhoek, for example, worked 12-hour shifts until their union negotiated 10-hour shifts, with overtime paid at one and a half times the normal hourly rate. Unions also bargain over conditions such as safety equipment, leave and training. A further role is protecting employment. When a firm plans job cuts, a union may press for alternatives - short-time working, moving workers to other posts, retraining, or voluntary rather than compulsory redundancy - and for fair selection and redundancy pay where cuts go ahead. It also represents members facing dismissal. Defending jobs protects members' incomes, though it can slow a firm's cost-cutting when its sales are falling.

blocks.heading: Influencing government policy
blocks.text: A further role reaches beyond the workplace: influencing government policy. Unions lobby ministers and members of parliament, make submissions when new labour laws are drafted, sit in talks between government, employers and unions, and run public campaigns. The issues are ones that affect workers across many firms at once: the level of a national minimum wage, the rules on hiring and dismissal, health and safety standards, and pensions. A better law wins for members in every workplace it covers, including those where the union is weak. In Namibia, union federations take part in such talks on labour law and wage policy; in the United Kingdom, unions campaigned for years for a national minimum wage before one was introduced. Their influence tends to be greater where they speak for many workers, and so many voters, and where the government wants their cooperation.

blocks.heading: Three boundaries worth learning
blocks.text: Three boundaries keep this topic clean. A trade union is not trade between nations: goods crossing borders belong to international trade, while the union's business is pay and conditions. A trade union is not a trade organisation: a body promoting a country's exports serves firms and the government, not workers' wages. And a question about unions' role in the economy asks what they do across the labour market, while a question about firms asks what happens inside one employer. The test: who acts, and on whose pay.
